core: Working definition of population health, attributed to Kindig and Stoddart (2003): the health outcomes of a group of individuals, including the distribution of such outcomes within the group
The group lens versus the individual lens: averages and patterns versus one person's story
The determinants idea: factors beyond medicine (behavior, environment, biology, systems) shape group health, named generally
Measuring the group: rates, proportions, averages, and comparisons, each named with one line
Why the group view matters: small shifts in a large group move many people, with an original illustrative example
Population health and public health: the connection between the lens and the field that acts on it
The honest framing: population health is about the curve of outcomes, not the outlier
supporting: Original illustrative arithmetic: a two-percent shift in a five-million-person region moves about one hundred thousand people
The distribution clause: equal averages can hide very different groups
Rose's high-risk versus population approach distinction as the scholarly backing for the group-view argument
outOfScope: Individual health versus population health as a full comparison (sibling topic public-health:foundations:individual-health-versus-population-health)
Social determinants of health detail and domains (sibling topic public-health:foundations:social-determinants-of-health)
Incidence as a measure (sibling topic public-health:foundations:incidence)
Prevalence as a measure (sibling topic public-health:foundations:prevalence)
Epidemiology methods, surveillance, and disparities/equity (sibling topics)

claims.claim: Population health is defined as the health outcomes of a group of individuals, including the distribution of such outcomes within the group (Kindig and Stoddart, 2003).
The field of population health includes health outcomes, patterns of health determinants, and the policies and interventions that link the two.
Because the definition of population health includes the distribution of outcomes, an unchanged group average can hide real movement within the group.
Most of a population's health is determined by non-medical root causes, the conditions of daily life, rather than by medical care alone.

A rate measures how often an event occurs in a defined population over a specified period of time, and rates put disease frequency in the perspective of population size, making comparison across locations, times, and groups possible.
A proportion compares a part to the whole, with the numerator included in the denominator; a ratio compares any two values and the values need not be related.

Epidemiology confronts two distinct questions: what determines individual cases and what determines how common a condition is in a group; the population approach seeks to control the causes of incidence, and it is not usually in competition with the high-risk approach.
Public health is a science-based, evidence-backed field that promotes and protects the health of all people and their communities.

conflictingEvidence: Kindig and Stoddart describe 'population health' as a relatively new term that had not yet been precisely defined at the time of writing; they proposed the outcomes-plus-distribution definition and invited critique. The lesson presents their definition as the attributed working definition, not as a settled universal one.

Sources use 'population health' and 'public health' inconsistently; some treat the terms as interchangeable, while Kindig and Stoddart explicitly differentiate population health from public health, health promotion, and social epidemiology. The lesson resolves this by presenting population health as the lens and public health as the field that acts on it (APHA).

Rose stresses that the high-risk and population approaches are complementary rather than competing; a common misreading is that the population view ignores high-risk individuals. The lesson states the complementarity explicitly.
rightsIssues: The Kindig and Stoddart article (AJPH 2003) and the Rose article are copyrighted; the lesson restates facts in original prose and keeps the single attributed definition phrase brief and quoted. WHO and APHA pages are reference-only. The CDC training manual is a U.S. government work (public domain).

sourceRecords.notes: Full text fetched and read 2026-08-22. Verified the proposed definition verbatim: 'the health outcomes of a group of individuals, including the distribution of such outcomes within the group,' plus the claim that the field includes health outcomes, patterns of health determinants, and policies and interventions linking the two, and the authors' explicit differentiation of population health from public health, health promotion, and social epidemiology.
